case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The First Circuit affirmed summary judgment for social workers and private child protection agencies sued under § 1983 by a Massachusetts father over their role in a sexual abuse investigation, holding that the familial-integrity right is too fact-dependent and unsettled to have been clearly established and that litigation communications were privileged.
key_cases.relevance: Frazier addresses the constitutional exposure of investigators, public and private, who conduct and act on a child sexual abuse investigation in Massachusetts.
key_cases.quote: Because this interest must always be balanced against the governmental interest involved, it is difficult, if not impossible, for officials to know when they have violated “clearly established” law.

key_cases.case_name: Lindsay v. Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The SJC clarified that on judicial review of a "supported" finding of abuse or neglect, the court asks only whether substantial evidence supports the hearing officer's conclusion that there was reasonable cause to believe the maltreatment occurred, and it upheld the supported finding of neglect.
key_cases.relevance: The standard Lindsay sets is the outcome measure against which the adequacy of the § 51B investigation is judged.
key_cases.quote: there need only be “substantial evidence” supporting the conclusion that there was “reasonable cause to believe” that Lindsay neglected Adrianna

key_cases.holding: The SJC affirmed a judgment dispensing with the mother's consent to the adoption of her two children, holding that the court investigator's reports were properly admitted and incorporated into the judge's findings, that those findings were not clearly erroneous, and that the mother's postadoption-visitation and ineffective-assistance claims were not preserved at trial and presented no exceptional circumstances warranting appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Mary holds that the court investigator's report, the product of the judicially ordered investigation, is admissible and may be incorporated into the judge's findings in a c. 210 proceeding as well as in care and protection.
key_cases.quote: Generally, issues not raised by a losing party in the trial court are not addressed on appeal, absent exceptional circumstances.

key_cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed a decree terminating the mother's parental rights, holding that a deceased DCF social worker's dictation notes and reports were admissible both as official records and as the declaration of a decedent, subject to the conditions that they be limited or redacted to facts rather than opinion, diagnosis or evaluation and that the author be available for cross-examination on request, and that second-level hearsay within them is admissible with opinion material edited out.
key_cases.relevance: Luc states the conditions on which the product of DCF's investigation - case work documents, dictation notes and reports - may be used as evidence against a parent.
key_cases.quote: The dictation notes and the reports were admissible subject to two conditions.

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours for the interim report and initial determination on the child's safety and custody (emergency response)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Initial contact on a screened-in 51A report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No penalty stated in M.G.L. c. 119, § 51B(c)

timeline_requirements.deadline: 5 business days (emergency response) or 15 business days (non-emergency response) for the written determination whether the abuse or neglect is substantiated
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Initial contact on a screened-in 51A report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No penalty stated in M.G.L. c. 119, § 51B; the 15-business-day determination may be extended only by a waiver approved by the DCF area director or requested by law enforcement (§ 51B(d))
